TCP: a reliable connection between two

TCP is a transport layer protocol (the other option is UDP). It is point-to-point: it connects exactly two devices, which is why it is not used for broadcast or multicast.

It is connection-oriented: first the connection is established, then data is exchanged, and finally it is released. And it is reliable, because it relies on:

  • Acknowledgments
  • Timeouts and retransmissions
  • Checksum of header and body

Its PDU is the segment, which usually travels inside a single IP datagram.
There is double error control: layer 2 does it between direct neighbors (a CRC that only detects); TCP does it between the two endpoints and also recovers.
Ports: which application am I talking to

A header is as large as the services the protocol offers: the TCP header is at least 20 bytes, in 32-bit words.

It starts with the source port and destination port (16 bits each): they identify the application within each host. There is always a client (it can be anyone) that connects to a well-known server: 443 HTTPS, 80 HTTP, 25 SMTP.

Each end of the connection is an endpoint: IP address + port.
The four values (client IP and port, server IP and port) identify the connection; that is why a single port can serve many connections.
One connection: 192.168.0.208 : 52326 (client endpoint, high port) ↔ 40.113.103.199 : 443 (server endpoint, well-known port).

For TCP, everything exchanged is one big sequence of bytes. The Sequence Number (32 bits) says which position in that sequence the segment's first byte occupies.

The Acknowledgment Number (32 bits) acknowledges what was received by indicating the next byte expected: after receiving bytes 1 to 10, the reply is ack = 11.

Acknowledgments are cumulative: the receiver can wait for three 10-byte segments and acknowledge them together with ack = 31.
TCP does not number segments: it counts bytes. An ack = n means "I received everything up to n − 1, I expect n."

Header length (4 bits): because of options, the header has variable length; it is measured in 32-bit words (5 = 20 bytes).

The flags, one bit each:

  • URG: there is urgent data (see Urgent pointer).
  • ACK: the acknowledgment field is valid.
  • PSH: process and respond right away, without delay (telnet).
  • RST: reset the connection.
  • SYN: synchronize sequence numbers.
  • FIN: I have no more data.

Window is the flow control field.
SYN, FIN, and RST explain how the connection is established and released.
In a SYN captured with Wireshark, Header length = 8: 8 × 4 = 32 bytes = 20 of fixed header + 12 of options (among them, MSS = 1460).
MSS: segments that don't need fragmenting

The MSS option (Maximum Segment Size) is declared when the connection is established, in the SYN segments, and does not change afterward. Each endpoint announces how large a segment can be:

MSS = interface MTU − 40 (20 bytes of IP header + 20 of TCP).

B is on Ethernet: 1500 − 40 = 1460. A goes out over SLIP: 296 − 40 = 256. Without MSS, B would build 1500-byte datagrams and the router would have to fragment them for the 296 link.
MSS only knows the endpoints' MTUs: if there is a smaller link along the path (for example, 1200), fragmentation happens there anyway.
A already knows its link is small and tells B: both build segments of up to 256 bytes and the router does not have to fragment.

The connection is established with three segments:

  • The client sends a SYN: a header with no data, with an initial sequence number x chosen at random.
  • The server accepts with SYN + ACK: its own number y, and ack = x + 1. If it does not accept, it replies RST.
  • The client answers ACK with ack = y + 1.

Wireshark shows relative numbers: if x = 90, you see seq = 0, and the server acknowledges 1 (actually, 91).
The SYN carries no data, but it is acknowledged as if it took up one byte: a byte that does not exist. The same happens with FIN.

Each endpoint keeps the connection's state.

Server: when a service starts, it asks TCP to listen on its port. This is the passive open: it goes from CLOSED to LISTEN. On receiving a SYN it replies SYN+ACK and stays in SYN_RCVD; with the client's ACK it reaches ESTABLISHED.

Client: an application asks to connect to an IP + port. This is the active open: it sends the SYN and goes to SYN_SENT; on receiving the SYN+ACK it sends the ACK and stays in ESTABLISHED.
The server was already waiting (passive); the one that takes the initiative and sends the SYN is the client (active).
Close: each endpoint closes its half

Once the exchange is finished, each endpoint closes its half:

  • The client sends FIN and goes to FIN_WAIT_1.
  • The server replies ACK and stays in CLOSE_WAIT; on receiving it, the client goes to FIN_WAIT_2: its half is already closed.
  • The server sends its FIN and goes to LAST_ACK.
  • The client replies ACK and stays in TIME_WAIT; with that ACK the server considers the connection finished.

On Windows, netstat lists TCP connections with their state.
A normal close takes four segments: FIN and ACK in one direction, FIN and ACK in the other.
Well-known ports and the firewall's role

Servers listen on well-known ports (below 1024) and have a stable IP; the client's port is usually above 1024. If a service runs on another port, it must be specified: address:8080.

The SYN is how a server exposes itself. That is why a firewall is configured to let through only SYNs addressed to the service's port (for example, 80); those going to any other port are silently dropped. Outbound, it lets out the SYNs the server generates.
Controlling SYNs means controlling who can open connections and to which port.
The firewall also keeps track of established connections: that way it lets through the non-SYN segments (data, ACK, FIN) of those connections.
TCP and its connection, at a glance

• Point-to-point, connection-oriented, and reliable; a second error control, end to end.
  • Port = application; endpoint = IP + port; four values = one connection.
  • Seq numbers bytes; cumulative ACK = next byte expected.
  • MSS = MTU − 40, declared in the SYN.
  • Open: SYN → SYN+ACK → ACK. Close: each endpoint closes its half with FIN + ACK.

One field remains unused: Window. In the next lesson we see how TCP uses it for flow control, and when it decides to retransmit.
